sentences.text: ## Pre-Training vs. Fine-Tuning: Concepts and Motivation
Building a large language model is not a single-step process.
Whether you are reading about GPT-4, experimenting with open-source models, or planning to deploy an LLM in a production system, you will encounter the same two-stage lifecycle again and again.
Understanding what each stage does—and why both exist—is foundational to everything that follows in this book.
This chapter unpacks that lifecycle in depth.
We will look at what pre-training actually accomplishes, why it is not always sufficient on its own, and when and how fine-tuning enters the picture.
Along the way, we will examine real-world case studies that illustrate why companies invest in fine-tuning rather than simply calling a general-purpose API.
### The Two-Stage Lifecycle
At the highest level, creating an LLM consists of two stages: pre-training and fine-tuning [c1, c9].
These two stages are not interchangeable—they serve fundamentally different purposes, operate on different kinds of data, and produce models with different capabilities.
[FIGURE: A horizontal pipeline diagram showing Stage 1 (Pre-training on raw text corpus → Base/Foundational Model) feeding into Stage 2 (Fine-tuning on labeled data → Task-Specific Model)]
Before diving into each stage, it helps to have a shared vocabulary.
Throughout this chapter, a *token* is approximately equal to one word [c13].
LLM stands for Large Language Model [c4].

And when we say *transformer*, we mean the neural network architecture that underlies models like GPT and BERT—though it is worth noting upfront that not all transformers are LLMs, and not all LLMs are transformers [c1304, c1308].
We will return to that distinction later in the chapter.
### Pre-Training: Building the Foundation
#### What Pre-Training Is
Pre-training means training an LLM on a huge amount of data so that it can perform a wide range of tasks [c23].
More precisely, it is the first training stage of an LLM, and the model it produces is called a *base model* or *foundational model* [c38].
Pre-training is also described simply as training on a large, diverse dataset [c1246].
The scale involved is difficult to overstate.
Pre-training requires a huge amount of data—billions or even trillions of words—and significant computational power, making it inaccessible to most individuals [c32].
LLMs are typically trained on billions of documents [c3165].
This is why pre-training is almost exclusively the domain of large research labs and well-funded companies.
#### The Training Objective: Next-Word Prediction
The core task that drives pre-training is deceptively simple. *Word completion* is the task where an LLM is given a set of words and must predict the next word [c18].
The model sees raw text—regular text without any labeling information [c37]—and learns by trying to predict what comes next, over and over, across billions of examples.
Intuitively, this seems like it should produce a model that is only good at finishing sentences.
The surprising empirical finding is that it produces much more than that.
#### Emergent Capabilities

LLMs trained only for next-word prediction can perform translation, multiple-choice questions, text summarization, sentiment analysis, linguistic acceptability, and question answering—without specific training on any of these tasks [c21].
In other words, the model learns to do far more than it was explicitly taught.
This is a sharp contrast with the traditional approach to NLP.

In traditional NLP, separate models must be trained for different tasks like translation, question answering, and emotion detection, whereas pre-trained LLMs can perform all these tasks with a single model [c22].
The pre-trained LLM is a generalist; the traditional pipeline is a collection of specialists.
Why does next-word prediction produce such broad capability?
The intuition is that to predict the next word accurately across a diverse corpus, the model must implicitly learn grammar, facts about the world, reasoning patterns, and even stylistic conventions.
The training signal is simple, but the knowledge required to satisfy it is vast.
LLMs interact effectively with users because they are trained on a huge and diverse set of data [c11].
That diversity is not incidental—it is the mechanism by which the model acquires general-purpose knowledge.
#### What Pre-Training Data Looks Like
Two commonly cited data sources illustrate the kind of material used in pre-training:

- **Common Crawl** is a huge and open repository of all the data on the internet [c16].
- **WebText2** is a corpus consisting of Reddit submissions, blog posts, Stack Overflow articles, and code [c17].
Together, these sources expose the model to an enormous variety of writing styles, topics, languages, and domains.
The breadth is intentional: the more diverse the training data, the more general the resulting model.
#### The Output: A Foundational Model
After pre-training, you have a base model.
GPT-4, for example, is a pre-trained model capable of text completion and other tasks such as sentiment analysis and question answering [c39].
GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformers [c1289], and it is explicitly a pre-trained or foundational model [c1290].
GPT generates one word at a time [c1293] and processes text from left to right, predicting only the rightmost unknown information [c1296].
This left-to-right, generative design is what makes GPT-style models well suited to text completion and open-ended generation.
[FIGURE: Diagram contrasting GPT (left-to-right, decoder-only, generates next token) with BERT (bidirectional, encoder-only, predicts masked tokens)]
For contrast, consider BERT—Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers [c1324].
BERT randomly masks some words during training and attempts to predict those masked words [c1292].
Rather than predicting the next word, BERT predicts hidden or masked words in a given sentence [c1291].
BERT is bidirectional, attending to different parts of the sentence from both left and right directions [c1297], and it uses only an encoder architecture without a decoder [c1326].

Because BERT can capture nuances and relationships between words by looking at the entire sentence from both directions [c1299], it can differentiate between different meanings of the same word—for example, "bank" as a financial institution versus "bank" as a river bank—by examining surrounding words [c1300].
This makes BERT particularly well suited to classification tasks: BERT is commonly used for sentiment analysis [c1301, c1327].
Both BERT and GPT have the word "transformers" in their names because they originated from the transformer architecture [c1303].
The original transformer architecture was developed for machine translation tasks, specifically translating English text into German and French [c1319].
The simplified transformer architecture consists of eight steps: tokenization, encoding, decoding with partial output, and word-by-word generation [c1320].
BERT uses an encoder architecture [c1295], while GPT uses a decoder-style design.
The key takeaway for this chapter is that pre-training—regardless of the specific architecture—produces a model with broad, general-purpose capabilities.
That is both its greatest strength and, in certain production contexts, its limitation.
### The Limits of Pre-Training Alone
A foundational model is powerful, but it is not always sufficient.
Pre-trained models like GPT-4 may not have access to company-specific data and therefore produce generic rather than domain-specific responses [c26].
Think about what this means in practice.
If you ask GPT-4 a question about your company's internal policies, your proprietary codebase, or the specific legal cases relevant to your jurisdiction, the model has no knowledge of those things.
It was trained on public internet data, not on your data.
Its answers will be plausible-sounding but generic—and in high-stakes domains, generic is not good enough.
This is the core motivation for fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning is needed when building applications specific to a particular task or domain, rather than for general-purpose use [c25].
General users and students can use pre-trained models like GPT-4 directly without fine-tuning, but companies and startups deploying LLM applications in production need fine-tuning [c36].
The distinction is worth sitting with.
If you are a student experimenting with language models, the base model is probably fine.
If you are building a product that will be used by real customers in a specific domain, you almost certainly need fine-tuning.
### Fine-Tuning: Specializing the Foundation
#### What Fine-Tuning Is
Fine-tuning is the second training stage.
Where pre-training operates on raw, unlabeled text at massive scale, fine-tuning typically requires a labeled dataset [c43].
The model has already learned general language understanding from pre-training; fine-tuning steers that understanding toward a specific task or domain.

The three main steps for building an LLM are: (1) training on a large corpus of raw text data, (2) pre-training to create a foundational model, and (3) fine-tuning on labeled data for specific tasks [c47].
Stage 3 of building an LLM involves fine-tuning on smaller, specific datasets to build applications such as classifiers or personal assistants [c3161].
Intuitively, fine-tuning is like hiring a generalist and then giving them specialized on-the-job training.
The generalist already knows how to read, write, reason, and communicate.
The specialized training teaches them the specific knowledge and conventions of your domain.
#### Types of Fine-Tuning
There are two main flavors of fine-tuning worth distinguishing at this stage.
**Instruction fine-tuning** involves providing instruction-answer pairs as labeled data to teach the model specific tasks like language translation [c41].
The training examples look like: "Translate the following sentence into French: [sentence]" → "[translation]".
The model learns to follow instructions by seeing many such pairs.

**Classification fine-tuning** adapts the model to produce categorical outputs—for example, labeling a piece of text as positive or negative sentiment, or routing a customer query to the correct department.
Fine-tuned LLMs can be used for specific tasks such as classification, summarization, translation, and building custom chatbots [c45].
Large companies building custom chatbots perform fine-tuning on foundational models rather than using foundational models alone [c46].
This is a consistent pattern across industries: the foundational model provides the language capability, and fine-tuning provides the domain knowledge and task alignment.
[FIGURE: Branching diagram showing a pre-trained base model being fine-tuned into multiple specialized models: a classifier, a summarizer, a translation model, and a custom chatbot]
### Real-World Case Studies
The motivation for fine-tuning becomes concrete when you look at how real organizations have deployed it.
The following three case studies illustrate different domains and different reasons for choosing fine-tuning over a general-purpose model.
#### SK Telecom: Customer Service in Korean

SK Telecom fine-tuned a model to improve customer service interactions for telecom-related conversations in Korean, resulting in a 35% increase in conversation summarization quality and a 33% increase in intent recognition accuracy [c27].
This case study highlights two important points.
First, domain specificity matters: telecom customer service has its own vocabulary, its own common issues, and its own conversational patterns.
A general-purpose model trained on English internet text is poorly positioned to handle Korean telecom conversations well.
Second, the improvements are measurable and substantial—35% and 33% are not marginal gains.
Fine-tuning produced a qualitatively better product for this specific use case.
#### Harvey: Legal AI

Harvey is an AI legal tool that was fine-tuned on legal case history data to assist attorneys and lawyers, addressing the limitation that foundational models lacked extensive knowledge of legal cases [c28].
The legal domain is a particularly clear example of why generic models fall short.
Legal reasoning depends on specific precedents, statutes, and jurisdictional rules.
A model that has not been trained on legal case history cannot reliably reason about those precedents.

Harvey's fine-tuning on legal case data directly addresses this gap—the model learns the specific knowledge that attorneys need, rather than relying on whatever legal content happened to appear in the pre-training corpus.
This also illustrates a risk management dimension.
In high-stakes professional contexts like law, a model that produces plausible-but-wrong answers is not just unhelpful—it is potentially harmful.
Fine-tuning on domain-specific data is one way to reduce that risk.
#### JPMorgan Chase: Proprietary Financial Data
JPMorgan Chase developed a fine-tuned AI-powered LLM suite specifically for their employees using their proprietary data, rather than relying solely on GPT-4 [c30].
This case study adds a dimension that the previous two do not: data privacy and competitive advantage.
A financial institution's proprietary data—trading strategies, client information, internal research—is not something that can or should be sent to a third-party API.
By fine-tuning their own model on their own data, JPMorgan Chase keeps that data in-house while still benefiting from the language capabilities of a large pre-trained model.
This pattern—fine-tune a foundational model on proprietary data, deploy internally—is increasingly common among large enterprises.

The foundational model provides the expensive, compute-intensive language understanding; the fine-tuning provides the domain-specific knowledge that makes the model useful for the organization's specific needs.
### Connecting the Stages: A Unified View
It is worth stepping back and seeing how pre-training and fine-tuning fit together as a coherent system.
Building a large language model from scratch typically proceeds in three stages: Stage 1 (understanding LLM basics), Stage 2 (pre-training), and Stage 3 (fine-tuning) [c3158].
The three main steps are: training on a large corpus of raw text data, pre-training to create a foundational model, and fine-tuning on labeled data for specific tasks [c47].
[FIGURE: Three-stage pipeline: Stage 1 (raw text corpus) → Stage 2 (pre-training → base model) → Stage 3 (fine-tuning on labeled data → specialized model)]
The relationship between the stages is not just sequential—it is also economical.
Pre-training is the expensive part.
It requires billions or trillions of tokens and massive computational resources [c32].
Fine-tuning, by contrast, operates on smaller, specific datasets [c3161].

By separating the two stages, the field has made it possible for organizations to benefit from the expensive pre-training work done by large labs, and then apply relatively affordable fine-tuning to adapt the result to their needs.
This division of labor is one of the most practically important ideas in applied LLM development.
You do not need to train a model from scratch to build a useful product.
You need to understand what the foundational model already knows, identify the gap between that and what your application requires, and close that gap through fine-tuning.
### When to Pre-Train vs. When to Fine-Tune
Given everything above, a practical question emerges: when should you do each?
The answer is almost always "fine-tune, don't pre-train from scratch"—unless you are a large research organization with the resources to do otherwise.
Pre-training requires a huge amount of data and significant computational power, making it inaccessible to most individuals [c32].
For the vast majority of practitioners, pre-training is something you consume (by downloading a foundational model) rather than something you perform.
Fine-tuning, on the other hand, is where most practitioners will spend their time.
The decision to fine-tune is driven by a few key factors:
1. **Domain specificity**: Does your application require knowledge that is unlikely to appear in general internet text?
Legal case history, proprietary financial data, and specialized technical documentation are all examples [c28, c30].
2. **Task specificity**: Does your application require a specific output format or behavior that a general-purpose model does not reliably produce?
Instruction fine-tuning can teach the model to follow specific formats [c41].
3. **Language and cultural specificity**: Does your application serve users in a specific language or cultural context that may be underrepresented in the pre-training data?
SK Telecom's Korean telecom use case is an example [c27].
4. **Data privacy**: Does your application require the model to reason about data that cannot be shared with a third-party API?
Fine-tuning on proprietary data, deployed internally, addresses this [c30].
If none of these factors apply—if you are a student, a researcher, or a developer building a general-purpose tool—then a pre-trained model used directly may be entirely sufficient [c36].
### The Broader Landscape: Transformers, LLMs, and Their Relationship
Before closing this chapter, it is worth clarifying a conceptual boundary that trips up many newcomers: the relationship between transformers and LLMs.
The terms "transformers" and "large language models" should not be used interchangeably, as they are different concepts [c1316].
Not all transformers are large language models [c1304], and not all large language models are based on transformer architecture [c1308].
Transformers can be used for computer vision tasks in addition to language tasks [c1305].

Vision Transformers (ViT) are transformer models applied to computer vision tasks such as image recognition and image classification [c1306], and they achieve comparable or better results than Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) while requiring substantially fewer computational resources for pre-training [c1307].
Transformers can also be used for image segmentation [c1330].
On the other side of the boundary, before transformers became dominant, other architectures were used for sequence modeling.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) maintain a feedback loop to incorporate memory [c1313], and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks incorporate two separate paths: one for short-term memories and one for long-term memories [c1314].
Both RNNs and LSTMs could perform sequence modeling and text completion tasks [c1312].
These are LLM-adjacent architectures that are not transformers.

The practical implication is that when you encounter a new model, you should not assume it is a transformer just because it is a language model, or assume it is a language model just because it uses transformer architecture.
The two concepts overlap substantially in current practice, but they are not identical.
### Summary
This chapter has covered the two-stage LLM lifecycle in depth.
Here are the key ideas to carry forward:
- **Pre-training** trains a model on a massive corpus of raw, unlabeled text using next-word prediction (or masked-word prediction, in the case of BERT) [c23, c43].
The result is a foundational model with broad, general-purpose capabilities [c38].

- **The emergent capabilities** of pre-trained models are remarkable: a model trained only on next-word prediction can perform translation, summarization, sentiment analysis, and question answering without task-specific training [c21].
- **The limitation** of pre-trained models is that they lack domain-specific knowledge and may produce generic responses when applied to specialized tasks [c26].
- **Fine-tuning** adapts a foundational model to a specific task or domain using labeled data [c43, c47].
It is needed for production applications in specialized domains [c25].
- **Real-world examples**—SK Telecom [c27], Harvey [c28], and JPMorgan Chase [c30]—demonstrate that fine-tuning produces measurable improvements in domain-specific performance.
- **Instruction fine-tuning** and **classification fine-tuning** are the two main approaches, suited to different output types [c41, c45].
- **Transformers and LLMs are related but distinct concepts** [c1316].
Not every transformer is an LLM, and not every LLM is a transformer [c1304, c1308].

In the next chapter, we will move from concepts to mechanics, beginning with the data preparation pipeline: how raw text is tokenized, how tokens are assigned IDs, and how those IDs are converted into the vector embeddings that an LLM actually processes [c3162, c3166, c3173].
